original_question: Let F be a finite field of characteristic p whose extension degree [F : F_p] is a power of 2. Is it impossible for any invertible exponent d over F to produce a three-valued Weil spectrum W_{F,d}?
target_in_paper: Section 10, Conjecture 10.6 (Helleseth Three-Valued Conjecture, 1971), with Theorem 10.7 immediately recording the proved characteristic-2 and characteristic-3 cases. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core content of the paper's official formulation: F is a finite field of characteristic p, the extension degree [F:F_p] is a power of 2, d ranges over invertible exponents over F, and the claim is that no such d should make the Weil spectrum three-valued. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
missing_details: The paper defines W_{F,d} as a function of a parameter a, namely W_{F,d}(a)=sum_{x in F} psi(x^d-ax), where psi(x)=exp(2 pi i Tr_{F/F_p}(x)/p) is the canonical additive character; your draft names W_{F,d} but does not define it. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))

The Weil spectrum is not the function W_{F,d} itself but the set {W_{F,d}(a): a in F^*}; the exclusion of a=0 is part of Definition 1.4, and the paper also notes that W_{F,d}(0)=0. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
Invertible exponent over F means a positive integer d with gcd(d,|F^*|)=1, equivalently gcd(d,|F|-1)=1. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))

Three-valued means that the spectrum {W_{F,d}(a): a in F^*} has exactly three distinct values. No separate nondegeneracy hypothesis needs to be added, because Theorem 10.2 says W_{F,d} is at least three-valued exactly when d is nondegenerate. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))

To match the paper exactly, this should be identified as Conjecture 10.6. The paper also states that Theorem 10.7 already proves the conjecture for p in {2,3}, so only the p>=5 cases remain open there. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))

Your wording says three-valued Weil spectrum W_{F,d}, but in the paper the notation W_{F,d} denotes the Weil-sum function and the spectrum is a separate object derived from it. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
refined_question: Let F be a finite field of characteristic p, let psi(x)=exp(2 pi i Tr_{F/F_p}(x)/p) be its canonical additive character, and let d be a positive integer with gcd(d,|F|-1)=1. For each a in F define W_{F,d}(a)=sum_{x in F} psi(x^d-ax), and call the associated Weil spectrum {W_{F,d}(a): a in F^*} three-valued if it has exactly three distinct elements. If [F:F_p] is a power of 2, must there be no invertible exponent d over F for which this Weil spectrum is three-valued? ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, if q=p^n with n a power of 2 and d is coprime to q-1, is the periodic crosscorrelation spectrum of a p-ary m-sequence of period q-1 and its decimation by d never three-valued? Section 3 shows that this crosscorrelation spectrum is obtained from the Weil spectrum by subtracting 1 from every value, so three-valuedness is preserved under the reformulation. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
justification: The draft is aiming at Helleseth's Three-Valued Conjecture rather than the neighboring symmetry conjecture (Conjecture 10.5) or the later classification problem (Open Problem 10.17), because its distinctive hypothesis is exactly that [F:F_p] be a power of 2 and its conclusion is the nonexistence of an invertible exponent giving a three-valued Weil spectrum. Definitions 1.1, 1.3, and 1.4 supply the missing notation and quantifiers, while Theorem 10.2 explains why no extra nondegeneracy assumption should be inserted. Theorem 10.7 is the adjacent partial resolution proving the statement for p=2 and p=3. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10090054))
